Executive Summary

The Governance Gap

Ghana's infrastructure deficit is not primarily a technical or financing problem — it is a governance and political economy problem. Patronage systems, rent-seeking intermediaries, and weak enforcement mechanisms perpetuate a status quo where 21 Ghanaians die every day from preventable WASH-related illness, 90% of solid waste goes uncollected, and the country's largest market operates on paper-based systems built decades ago.

Summary — Infrastructure & Basic Services

BRIDGE's infrastructure thesis begins with a single observation: solutions that compete for conventional infrastructure contracts will fail. The procurement systems are captured. The incentives are misaligned. The political economy resists transparent delivery.

BRIDGE's approach is different. Rather than competing for contracts, BRIDGE creates asset-backed platforms that bundle service delivery with transparent governance, community accountability, and data-driven performance monitoring. The Kejetia Market Digital Platform is the proof of concept — a $17M direct operation at West Africa's largest single market, demonstrating that infrastructure can serve 10,000+ vendors while generating the 15–20% IRR that makes it replicable.

The 2026 budget's GH₵30B Big Push Infrastructure Programme and the Model Markets mandate allocating GH₵2.2B (25% of DACF) across 260+ districts create the government co-investment infrastructure that BRIDGE's approach has been waiting for. The policy validates BRIDGE's integrated service delivery model and creates a clear pathway from Kejetia flagship to national scale.

Section OneThe Scale of the Crisis

Water, Sanitation & the Daily Death Toll

Ghana's WASH deficit is not a natural condition — it is the accumulated result of governance failures, funding collapse, and systemic neglect of the infrastructure that keeps citizens alive.

87.7% of Ghanaians have access to basic water services. Only 44.4% have safely managed water. That 43-point gap — between access and safety — is where 7,653 people a year die. It is also where BRIDGE operates.

Fig 01 · WASH Coverage — Ghana's Access Gap to Universal Service
Current WASH coverage vs. universal service target. Dark bars show current access; grey shows the remaining gap. Note: 72% open defecation rate in the Northern Region against a 23% national average — the geographic concentration of risk. Source: WaterAid Ghana; UNICEF WASH Monitoring; Ghana NDPC 2024.

The Funding Collapse

The most alarming trend in Ghana's infrastructure landscape is not the access gap itself — it is the speed with which government commitment has evaporated. In 2022, the government financed 27% of WASH expenditure. By 2024, that figure had collapsed to 5%. Donor dependency now stands at 95%.

This is not a fiscal crisis — it is a political economy failure. Infrastructure spending that does not generate visible ribbon-cutting moments or create procurement opportunities for politically connected contractors gets systematically defunded. The communities who depend on boreholes, drainage, and sanitation have no lobbying power. They have no constituency office. They have numbers: 7,653 deaths per year from diseases that clean water prevents.

Fig 02 · WASH Funding Source — Government Contribution Collapse
Government share of WASH funding 2022–2024. Source: Ghana Ministry of Finance; WaterAid Ghana 2024.
Ghana's infrastructure deficit is not a technical problem or a financing problem. It is a governance problem. Solutions that ignore the patronage systems and weak enforcement mechanisms that perpetuate the status quo will fail regardless of capital availability.

Section TwoThe Flagship

Kejetia — Where the Model Lives

West Africa's largest single market. 10,000+ vendors. $507M in government construction investment. Operating on paper. BRIDGE changes that.

Kejetia Market in Kumasi is not just an infrastructure opportunity — it is the proof-of-concept location for everything BRIDGE believes about how infrastructure should work. The government has invested over $507M in physical construction across two phases. The market generates hundreds of millions in annual trade. And every single vendor still records transactions on paper, restocks from memory, and has no digital presence beyond the stall they physically occupy.

Fig 03 · Kejetia Digital Platform — Three-Phase Deployment & Vendor Scale
Capital deployed per phase (bars, left axis) vs. vendor platform adoption (line, right axis). Phase 3 targets 10,000 active vendors at 80%+ monthly active rate — the threshold for platform sustainability via transaction-based revenue. Source: BRIDGE Infrastructure Sector Analysis, 2026.

What the Platform Does

BRIDGE establishes Kejetia Digital Markets Ltd. as a wholly-owned subsidiary deploying a vendor-first platform that transforms operations in three dimensions:

DimensionTransformation
InventoryDigital tracking replaces memory-based restocking. Reduces stockouts, ties up less capital, enables demand forecasting.
PaymentsMobile money integration ends cash-only transactions. Reduces theft risk, enables credit building, unlocks insurance products.
Market AccessOnline marketplace extends vendor reach beyond physical stall. Customers find vendors remotely; delivery becomes possible.
Supply ChainAggregated purchasing eliminates per-vendor middleman extraction. Bulk discounts. Direct producer connections.
Financial IdentityTransaction history builds credit scores. Opens access to formal banking, vendor loans, and business insurance for the first time.
10,000 vendor families achieving economic stability. 8,000 children accessing better education funded by increased incomes. A market becoming a source of pride rather than a source of frustration.
BRIDGE Kejetia Impact Framework — Peace & Prosperity Outcomes
Why Direct Operation

BRIDGE operates Kejetia directly rather than investing in a third party. Strategic importance demands control. The platform is proof-of-concept infrastructure for BRIDGE's national replication model — it cannot be delegated to a partner whose incentives may not align with the 260-district scale ambition.

Target Economics

$17M over 3 years. 15–20% IRR from efficiency gains, platform transaction revenues, and vendor service fees. Break-even at Phase 3 scale (10,000 vendors at GH₵15–25/month platform fee). Government partnership through Model Markets mandate provides co-investment structure.

Section ThreeComparative Position

Ghana vs. The Region

Ghana outperforms some peers and underperforms others — the pattern reveals where the investment case is strongest.

Fig 04 · Infrastructure Access — Ghana vs. Sub-Saharan Africa Average
Ghana vs. Sub-Saharan Africa average across five infrastructure dimensions. Ghana leads on power but lags significantly on sanitation and solid waste management — the sectors with the highest mortality cost. Source: WHO; World Bank; Ghana Statistical Service 2024.

The Urban Flooding Crisis

Recent research has established something important: Ghana's urban flooding is primarily a governance failure, not a climate phenomenon. In a 2025 study of Accra flooding, 52% of households attributed floods to weak enforcement of land use regulations. No statistical correlation was found between increased rainfall and flooding incidence.

Between 2008 and 2018, encroachment on major wetlands — Densu Delta, Sakumo Lagoon, Songor Lagoon — accelerated dramatically. The floods are predictable. The damage is preventable. And the communities losing livelihoods, inventory, and homes to recurrent flooding disproportionately include market traders and peri-urban residents — the exact population BRIDGE's market infrastructure investments serve.

The Waste Opportunity

Ghana generates 12,710 tonnes of solid waste daily. Only 10% is properly collected. The recyclable waste potential is valued at GH₵83 billion annually — an asset being buried, burned, or dumped rather than converted into economic value. BRIDGE's Waste-to-Compost venture targets this gap.

Roads — The Last 49%

Only 49% of Ghana's road network is maintained. The unmaintained 51% — concentrated in feeder roads serving rural markets and agricultural areas — directly undermines the return on every other BRIDGE sector investment. Without farm-to-market roads, cold storage becomes irrelevant. Without market access roads, vendor platforms become theoretical.

Section FourPolicy Window

The 2026 Budget — A Co-Investment Moment

The GH₵30B Big Push Programme is the largest single infrastructure commitment in Ghana's recent history — and it maps directly to BRIDGE's operating model.

The Mahama administration's Build24 pillar represents a generational infrastructure commitment. But the most strategically significant line item for BRIDGE is not the GH₵30B headline — it is the Model Markets mandate that commits 25% of the District Assemblies Common Fund to 24-Hour Market development across 260+ districts.

Fig 05 · 2026 Infrastructure Budget Allocations — BRIDGE Entry Points
Key 2026 budget allocations with BRIDGE venture alignment. The Model Markets mandate (DACF 25%) is the flagship BRIDGE opportunity — Kejetia becomes the national template. Source: Ghana Ministry of Finance, 2026 Budget Statement.

The Model Markets Pathway

The Model Markets policy creates a three-stage scaling pathway that turns BRIDGE's Kejetia investment into a national platform:

StageTimelineScope
Stage 1
Flagship Demo		2026Complete Kejetia Market Resilience Platform. Develop standardized specifications and governance frameworks suitable for replication.
Stage 2
Regional Hubs		2027–2028Expand to 3–5 major markets: Makola, Asafo, Tamale Central, Takoradi. Train local teams. Establish management companies per market.
Stage 3
National Scale		2029+Franchise model enabling district assemblies to deploy BRIDGE-designed market systems using DACF allocations. 260+ districts.
Q1 2026 — Critical Entry

BRIDGE must formally apply as preferred service delivery partner under the Model Markets mandate before district assemblies commit DACF allocations to alternative providers. The window is open now — first-mover positioning cannot be recovered once district procurement cycles begin.

DACF Integration Model

BRIDGE can approach District Assemblies with integrated packages that coordinate across multiple DACF allocations — a Model Market that integrates CHPS compound, vocational training, and WASH infrastructure, drawing from market (25%), health (10%), education (10%), and water (10%) allocations simultaneously.

Section SevenRisk Analysis

Risk & Mitigation

Infrastructure risk in Ghana is primarily political and governance risk — BRIDGE's asset-backed, performance-monitored, community-accountable model is specifically designed to manage it.

Risk Category Severity BRIDGE Mitigation Strategy
Political Economy / PatronageHIGHAsset-backed direct operation removes BRIDGE from procurement capture. Platform revenue model creates government interest in BRIDGE success rather than competitor preference. Transparent performance data creates community accountability that political interference cannot easily override.
Government Policy ReversalMEDIUMModel Markets mandate is structurally embedded in DACF — constitutionally protected fund. Market vendor community (10,000+ at Kejetia alone) becomes political constituency for platform continuation. Long-term service contracts survive government transitions.
Vendor AdoptionMEDIUMVendor-first design with on-site training staff and peer educator program. Multi-language materials (Twi, Ga, English). Phase 1 pilot with 1,000 vendors validates adoption before full deployment. Revenue model requires vendor success — incentive alignment is structural.
Power Infrastructure DependencyMEDIUMSolar micro-grid (Venture ③) provides independent power for the digital platform. ECG unreliability is designed out of the system rather than relied upon.
Replication Quality ControlMEDIUMStandardized technical specifications, governance frameworks, and management systems developed at Kejetia before replication begins. BRIDGE-trained management companies per market maintain quality standards. Market Replication Fund (Venture ⑪) finances only BRIDGE-specification deployments.
Community ResistanceLOWKejetia community engagement is established — Kumasi Metropolitan Assembly and vendor associations are partners, not subjects. Market authority trust built through demonstrated service improvements before replication begins.

Section EightSystem Integration

Infrastructure as Enabler

Infrastructure is not a sector — it is the prerequisite for every other sector. Without reliable power, markets, roads, and WASH, every other BRIDGE investment underperforms.

Kejetia is not just BRIDGE's flagship infrastructure investment. It is the integration hub for Financial Inclusion (mobile money rails), Technology (digital platform), Agriculture (vendor market access), and every sector whose beneficiaries pass through a market. Infrastructure is the common thread that ties the BRIDGE portfolio into a system.

BRIDGE Sector Infrastructure Integration
Financial InclusionKejetia transaction data builds vendor credit scores — the financial identity layer that opens access to formal banking. Mobile money integration on the platform IS the Financial Inclusion sector deployed at market scale.
Health SystemsWASH infrastructure for CHPS compounds; reliable power for health facility cold chains and diagnostic equipment; market WASH reducing the disease burden that health sector must treat. DACF health allocation (10%) co-funds the same infrastructure that serves markets.
Technology & InnovationThe Kejetia Digital Platform is a Technology sector investment deployed through Infrastructure. IoT monitoring, smart meters, and platform analytics are Technology ventures that use Infrastructure as their delivery vehicle.
Education & SkillsWASH and power for school facilities; infrastructure maintenance training creating TVET pathways; engineering apprenticeships through BRIDGE infrastructure operations. DACF education (10%) co-funds the same district-level infrastructure BRIDGE manages.
Agriculture & Value ChainsCold storage network in markets connects agricultural cold chain to urban consumer. Feeder road maintenance (Venture ⑫) directly de-risks agricultural market access. Kejetia agricultural vendor section is the urban endpoint of the agriculture value chain.
Manufacturing & IndustryReliable power and water for processing facilities; industrial infrastructure for manufacturing parks; Waste-to-Compost output serves agricultural manufacturing as organic input supply.
Transportation & LogisticsMarket infrastructure and road maintenance directly support logistics efficiency. Kejetia supply chain optimization reduces transport costs for every vendor on the platform. Connect24's GH₵4.3B road budget directly de-risks BRIDGE market access investments.
Tourism & HospitalityKejetia and upgraded markets become tourism destinations in their own right — clean, digitized, navigable. Reliable utilities for hospitality sector. WASH infrastructure in tourist areas is a hospitality product, not a development project.

The Kejetia Market Digital Platform is BRIDGE's proof of concept for an entire theory of change: that transparent, accountable, asset-backed infrastructure investment can serve Ghanaian citizens at scale, generate competitive financial returns, and create the digital and physical foundation upon which every other sector investment compounds.
